doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: State of women in jazz today
summary: Responding to Karolina Strassmayer's quote, Rowe says things are improving, with more young women and record Sisters in Jazz applicants, though not level.

venues.name: Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How do you feel about the state of women in jazz right now? I’m going to read a quote from Karolina Strassmayer. She was talking about the expectations of a woman and “How can I embody the spirit of jazz if I’m concerned whether people like me or they think that I’m pretty or they think that I’m nice. So I found that there’s a contradiction between my socialization as a girl, as a woman, and the music I play.”

Well of course needless to say I think about this constantly, you know especially with trying to get a lot of young women in our program which we’ve been, I’ll say I’ve been pretty good at. I think we have nine or ten women in our program of 55 students, and that’s without a jazz vocal program, so these are all instrumentalists. Yeah I think that’s an ongoing concern for younger women. I think it’s less of a concern than it was 30, 40 years ago. I see a lot of my younger women students are just really gung-ho and I’m going to be who I’m going to be and if the guys don’t like it that’s too bad and you know, things like that, which I think is great. Because the guys don’t have to worry about that. I think the situation for women in jazz is getting better and better by the day. I mean we still have plenty of issues, you know just around looking after ourselves and you know safely and you know there’s still, well I don’t need to go into it but there’s still issues of women not being treated as respectfully as they should be in many different types of ways. But I see a lot more young women playing, getting the encouragement to play. We had the most applicants for the Sisters in Jazz Collegiate Combo Competition which I oversee for the Jazz Education Network this year that we had — I think we had over 50,

which is great. And that’s a really positive, positive sign. So I think things are improving. I think a lot more is being written about it. There’s more awareness, and I counsel my young women to be strong and stick up for themselves and play the music they want to play, express themselves the way they want to play. But yeah, it’s still hard. I mean it’s not quite a level playing field.
